\section[olá]{olá — \textquotedblleft{}hi\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-ola}



\begin{quote}
The friendly Portuguese \textquotedblleft{}hi\textquotedblright{} — one of the few words with no clean Latin root.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{olá} = \emph{oh-LAH} — stress on the second syllable (the accent on \emph{á} marks it); clear \emph{l}, open \emph{a}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{olá} is a friendly interjection of uncertain birth — probably a natural call for attention (like English \emph{hello/hallo}), perhaps reinforced by Arabic \emph{w-Allāh} (\textquotedblleft{}by God\textquotedblright{}) in the centuries of Moorish Iberia. Unlike most Portuguese words, it has \emph{no} clean Latin root: some greetings are just sounds. Spanish, its close sibling, has the near-identical \emph{hola}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{olá} is friendly and fairly neutral — fine for most people; for real formality you add \emph{bom dia} / \emph{boa tarde} (built next). In Brazil you'll also hear \emph{oi} for a casual \textquotedblleft{}hi.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Writing — follow the greeting you can see}
Keep \textbf{olá} visible. Point to the acute accent over \textbf{á}; it marks the stressed last syllable. Trace the word once from \textbf{o} to \textbf{á}, then say \emph{oh-LAH}.

This is not a spelling test. Your eye and hand are only following one greeting whose sound and meaning are still on the page.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}olá\textquotedblright{} (\emph{oh-LAH})
  \item the casual Brazilian alternative — \textquotedblleft{}oi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{olá} have a Latin root, and what Spanish word is its twin? (No — it's a natural interjection; Spanish \emph{hola}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[bom / boa]{bom / boa — \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-bom}



\begin{quote}
The word that starts \emph{bom dia}, \emph{boa tarde}, \emph{boa noite}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bom} is \textbf{nasal}: \emph{bõ}, the \emph{m} not fully closed, the vowel through the nose. \textbf{boa} (feminine) is a clear \emph{BOH-ah}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bom / boa} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{bonus / bona} $\to$ English \textbf{bon}us, \textbf{bon}anza. Spanish, another daughter of Latin, made \emph{bueno / buena}; Portuguese wore \emph{bonus} down further, to the little nasal \emph{bom}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it agrees with the noun}]
\textbf{bom / boa} changes to match its noun: \emph{bom} (m.), \emph{boa} (f.), \emph{bons / boas} (pl.) — Latin's adjective agreement, alive across the Romance family. So it's \emph{bom dia} (m.) but \emph{boa tarde} (f.).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bom\textquotedblright{} (nasal \emph{bõ}), \textquotedblleft{}boa\textquotedblright{} (\emph{BOH-ah})
  \item why \emph{bom dia} but \emph{boa tarde} (gender)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \textbf{bom} from, and why \emph{bom dia} but \emph{boa tarde}? (\emph{bonus}; \emph{dia} is masculine, \emph{tarde} feminine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o / a]{o / a — \textquotedblleft{}the,\textquotedblright{} an article worn to a single letter}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-o-a}



\begin{quote}
Before your first noun: \textquotedblleft{}the.\textquotedblright{} Portuguese wore it down further than any of its sisters.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{o} (masculine \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{a} (feminine) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{ille / illa} (\textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{}). Portuguese did something striking — it eroded the word \emph{further than any sibling}:

\begin{quote}
Latin \textbf{ille} $\to$ Italian \textbf{il} $\to$ Spanish \textbf{el} $\to$ Portuguese just \textbf{o}.
\end{quote}

The whole pointing-word has worn down to a single vowel. (English \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} is Germanic, unrelated.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two genders}]
Every Portuguese noun is \textbf{masculine or feminine} — Latin's genders collapsed to two. Learn each noun \emph{with} its article: \textbf{o} (m.), \textbf{a} (f.). Watch the trap next: \emph{o dia} (\textquotedblleft{}the day\textquotedblright{}) is masculine even though it ends in \emph{-a}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}o\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}
  \item the erosion — \emph{ille} $\to$ \emph{il} $\to$ \emph{el} $\to$ \emph{o}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gave Portuguese \textbf{o}, and how is it unusual among its sisters? (\emph{ille}; Portuguese wore it down to a single letter, more than \emph{il/el}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dia]{dia — \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-dia}



\begin{quote}
Your first noun — and a gender trap.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{o dia} (masc.) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{dies} (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}), taken almost straight, like Spanish \emph{día}. Cousins from \emph{dies}: \textbf{di}urnal, \textbf{di}ary; and, through the derived \emph{diurnum}, English \textbf{jour}nal and \textbf{jour}ney (which is why Italian \emph{giorno} and French \emph{jour} look so different — they took the longer road, Portuguese and Spanish the short one).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a gender trap}]
\emph{dia} ends in \emph{-a} — the usual \textbf{feminine} signal — yet it is \textbf{masculine}: \emph{o dia}. A fossil of its Latin origin (\emph{dies} was masculine), and a reminder to learn each noun \emph{with its article} rather than guessing gender from the ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}o dia\textquotedblright{} (masculine, despite the \emph{-a})
  \item cousins — \emph{diary}, \emph{diurnal}, \emph{journal}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gave \textbf{dia}, and why is \emph{o dia} a trap? (\emph{dies}; it's masculine even though it ends in \emph{-a}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bom dia]{bom dia — \textquotedblleft{}good morning,\textquotedblright{} assembled}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-bom-dia}



\begin{quote}
Put the pieces together into the polite morning hello.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item bom (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) + dia (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{bom dia} = \textquotedblleft{}good day\textquotedblright{} $\to$ in practice, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{}} (used until noon).
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{bom dia} is the polite, all-purpose morning hello — safe with anyone. After midday it gives way to \emph{boa tarde}, and after dark to \emph{boa noite}. (Spanish pluralises the blessing — \emph{buenos días} — where Portuguese keeps it singular, \emph{bom dia}.)
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bom dia\textquotedblright{} (nasal \emph{bõ} + \emph{dia})
  \item the day's arc — bom dia $\to$ boa tarde $\to$ boa noite
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words make \textbf{bom dia}, and when is it used? (\emph{bom} + \emph{dia}; morning, until noon.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tarde / boa tarde]{tarde / boa tarde — \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-tarde}



\begin{quote}
The afternoon greeting — named, like its Spanish twin, after \emph{lateness}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a tarde} (fem.) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{tardus} (\textquotedblleft{}slow, late\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{tardus} behind English \textbf{tard}y and re\textbf{tard} (\textquotedblleft{}to slow\textquotedblright{}). Portuguese named the afternoon after its \emph{lateness}, exactly as Spanish did with the identical \emph{tarde}. \textbf{boa tarde} = \textquotedblleft{}good afternoon\textquotedblright{} (\emph{boa}, feminine, because \emph{tarde} is feminine).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}boa tarde\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousin — English \emph{tardy} (late)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gave \textbf{tarde}, and what English word shares it? (\emph{tardus}, \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}; \emph{tardy}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[noite / boa noite]{noite / boa noite — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} and the \emph{-ct-} $\to$ \emph{-it-} rule}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-noite}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Night\textquotedblright{} — and a sound-rule shared with French.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a noite} (fem.) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{noctem} (\emph{noct-}) $\to$ English \textbf{noct}urnal, equi\textbf{nox}. Portuguese turned Latin \emph{-ct-} into \textbf{-it-} (\emph{noite}) — the same change French made (\emph{nuit}), while Spanish went \emph{-ch-} (\emph{noche}) and Italian \emph{-tt-} (\emph{notte}):

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{Portuguese} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{French} & \textbf{Italian} \\
\midrule
\emph{noctem} & no\textbf{it}e & no\textbf{ch}e & nu\textbf{it} & no\textbf{tt}e \\
\emph{factum} & fe\textbf{it}o & he\textbf{ch}o & fa\textbf{it} & fa\textbf{tt}o \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{boa noite} = \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} — used both as an evening greeting and the farewell for bed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}boa noite\textquotedblright{}
  \item the rule — Latin \emph{-ct-} $\to$ Portuguese \emph{-it-} (\emph{noite}, \emph{feito})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word gave \textbf{noite}, and what sound-change does it show? (\emph{noctem}; \emph{-ct-} $\to$ \emph{-it-}, like French \emph{nuit}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[obrigado / obrigada]{obrigado / obrigada — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}{[}I am{]} obliged\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-obrigado}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Thanks\textquotedblright{} — and, uniquely, the word changes with \emph{who is speaking}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{obrigado} $\approx$ \emph{oh-bree-GAH-doo} — the final \emph{-o} sounds like \emph{u}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{obrigado / obrigada} (\textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{obligātus} (\textquotedblleft{}bound, obliged\textquotedblright{}), from \emph{ob-} (\textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{ligāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to bind\textquotedblright{}). It is the \emph{same} word as English \textbf{obligated}, and shares its root with \textbf{oblige}, \textbf{oblig}ation, and (via \emph{ligare}) \textbf{lig}ament and \textbf{li}able. To say \emph{obrigado} is to say \textquotedblleft{}I am \textbf{bound} to you\textquotedblright{} — indebted by your kindness.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it agrees with the \emph{speaker}}]
Because \emph{obrigado} literally means \textquotedblleft{}{[}I am{]} obliged,\textquotedblright{} it takes the gender of \textbf{whoever is speaking}: a man says \textbf{obrigado}, a woman says \textbf{obrigada} — no matter who they're thanking. This is unlike ordinary adjectives (which match their noun); here the adjective matches \emph{you}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}obrigado\textquotedblright{} (if you're male) / \textquotedblleft{}obrigada\textquotedblright{} (if female)
  \item the meaning — \textquotedblleft{}I am obliged / bound to you\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousin — English \emph{obligated}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{obrigado} literally mean, and how does a woman say it? (\textquotedblleft{}I am obliged\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{obligātus}; \emph{obrigada} — it agrees with the speaker.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — the day of greetings}

\label{lesson:PT-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words today. Everything below is something you have already met, said once, and can now put in one place.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the day of greetings}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Portuguese} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{olá} & hi \\
\emph{bom dia} & good morning \\
\emph{boa tarde} & good afternoon \\
\emph{boa noite} & good night \\
\emph{obrigado / obrigada} & thank you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every piece traced:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bom} $\leftarrow$ \emph{bonus}
  \item \textbf{dia} $\leftarrow$ \emph{dies} (masculine, despite the \emph{-a})
  \item \textbf{tarde} $\leftarrow$ \emph{tardus} (\textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}; English \emph{tardy})
  \item \textbf{noite} $\leftarrow$ \emph{noctem}, via \emph{-ct-} $\to$ \emph{-it-} (like French \emph{nuit})
  \item \textbf{obrigado} $\leftarrow$ \emph{obligātus} (\textquotedblleft{}obliged\textquotedblright{}; English \emph{obligated})
\end{itemize}

And two Portuguese habits: the article eroded to a single vowel (\textbf{o / a}), and \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} agrees with the \textbf{speaker} (\emph{obrigado} m. / \emph{obrigada} f.).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five greetings
  \item greet and thank — \textquotedblleft{}bom dia!\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}obrigado/obrigada.\textquotedblright{}
  \item why a woman says \emph{obrigada}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say all five greetings. Why does \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} have two forms? (It means \textquotedblleft{}{[}I am{]} obliged,\textquotedblright{} so it matches the speaker: \emph{obrigado} / \emph{obrigada}.) What did the Latin article \emph{ille} erode to in Portuguese? (A single letter, \emph{o}.)

Next chapter: introducing yourself — \emph{o meu nome é…} / \emph{chamo-me…} — and Portuguese's \emph{tu} vs. \emph{você} (familiar / polite \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}).
\end{tcolorbox}
